concept.name: Memory Models & Happens-Before

relationships.description: Connects Memory Models & Happens-Before to python concurrency nogil in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: A memory model defines the exact rules under which writes by one CPU core become visible to another, using a formal partial order called happens-before to constrain compiler reordering, CPU store buffers, and out-of-order execution.
spark.keyTakeaway: Cache coherence (MESI) guarantees cores eventually agree on a single address, not the order of writes across different addresses; only explicit happens-before edges (release/acquire, mutexes, volatile) prevent stale reads on ARM and x86.

concept.whyItMatters: Modern compilers (`-O2`/`-O3`) and CPUs aggressively reorder independent loads and stores to hide 50–100 ns DRAM latency. Code that passes 100% of unit tests on an x86-64 laptop (Total Store Order) can silently corrupt state or read half-initialized structs when deployed to AWS Graviton or Apple Silicon (ARMv8 weak memory ordering) if it relies on data races instead of formal happens-before synchronization.
whenToUse: Implementing lock-free data structures (ring buffers, SPSC/MPSC queues, epoch-based reclamation) using `std::atomic` or Java `VarHandle`.
Publishing immutable configuration snapshots or lookup tables via atomic pointer swaps (`release` store paired with `acquire` load) without taking a reader lock.
Auditing cross-platform concurrency code migrating from x86-64 servers to ARM64 (AWS Graviton, Ampere) where store-store and load-load reordering are exposed.
whenNotToUse: Standard business logic and I/O-bound microservices where a `Mutex`, `RwLock`, or message-passing channel costs ~15–25 ns and eliminates memory-ordering bugs completely.
Replacing `memory_order_seq_cst` with `relaxed` or `acquire/release` prematurely without a benchmark proving atomic fence overhead is a real bottleneck.
Single-threaded event loops (Node.js, Redis main thread, Tokio `LocalSet`) where no shared memory is accessed concurrently across OS threads.
keyPoints: Happens-before (`A ->hb B`) is a transitive partial order: if A happens-before B, all memory effects of A are guaranteed visible to B, regardless of physical clock time.
Program order alone only establishes happens-before within a single thread; cross-thread visibility requires a synchronizes-with edge (mutex unlock->lock, atomic release->acquire, thread spawn/join).
x86-64 implements Total Store Order (TSO): it preserves Store-Store and Load-Load order automatically, only allowing Store-Load reordering via per-core store buffers.
ARMv8 and POWER implement weak memory models: independent loads and stores can reorder freely in hardware, requiring `LDAR`/`STLR` or `DMB ISH` barriers (~3–30 ns).
Data races (two threads accessing the same non-atomic location concurrently, at least one writing) are Undefined Behavior in C/C++ and allow compilers to tear reads or hoist checks out of loops.

examples.title: SPSC Ring Buffer Corruption on AWS Graviton (ARM64)
examples.scenario: A low-latency C++ telemetry collector used `memory_order_relaxed` for both payload writes and the ring-buffer `head` index update; it ran flawlessly for two years on Intel Xeon (x86 TSO) because stores never reordered.
examples.outcome: After migrating to AWS Graviton3 (ARM64), consumers intermittently read zeroed/stale payloads because ARM reordered the `head` index store ahead of the payload write. Changing `head` to `release`/`acquire` fixed the corruption with <1% throughput impact.

examples.title: Java Double-Checked Locking Without `volatile`
examples.scenario: A high-throughput Java service cached a singleton `Config` object using double-checked locking on a non-`volatile` field to avoid synchronization overhead.
examples.outcome: Under JIT C2 compilation, the reference assignment was reordered before the constructor's field writes completed, exposing partially initialized fields (`null` maps) to concurrent threads. Adding `volatile` established a write-to-read happens-before edge.

tradeOffs.pro: Sequential consistency (`seq_cst`) enforces a single global total order across all atomic variables, preventing subtle Dekker/Peterson store-load anomalies.
tradeOffs.con: On x86, `seq_cst` stores emit `XCHG` or `MFENCE` (~20–40 ns stall); on ARMv8, `STLR`+`LDAR` adds full-barrier ordering overhead compared to `acquire`/`release`.

tradeOffs.pro: `relaxed` compiles to plain `MOV`/`LDR`/`STR` instructions with zero hardware fence overhead, ideal for independent counters and statistics.
tradeOffs.con: `relaxed` provides atomicity (no torn reads) and per-variable modification order, but zero happens-before guarantees for surrounding non-atomic memory.

tradeOffs.pro: Lock-free `acquire`/`release` paths avoid OS scheduler preemption, priority inversion, and kernel `futex` sleeps under light contention.
tradeOffs.con: Correctness proofs require formal tools (CDSChecker, Loom, TLA+) and subtle ABA or memory-reclamation bugs are far harder to debug than a mutex.

failureModes.name: Store-Buffer Reordering (Dekker's Anomaly)
failureModes.description: Even on x86 TSO, Thread 1 writes `X=1` then reads `Y`, while Thread 2 writes `Y=1` then reads `X`. Both reads hit L1 cache before either store drains from its core's store buffer, so both threads read `0`.
failureModes.mitigation: Use `memory_order_seq_cst` (which flushes the store buffer via `LOCK`/`MFENCE` on x86) whenever two threads must observe each other's writes in a mutually exclusive pattern.

failureModes.name: Compiler Loop Hoisting on Non-Atomic Flags
failureModes.description: A thread polls `while (!ready) {}` on a plain `bool`. Under `-O2`, GCC/Clang proves `ready` isn't modified inside the loop, hoists the read once into a register, and hangs forever.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use `std::atomic<bool>` (or `volatile` in Java, `atomic.Bool` in Go)—never use C/C++ `volatile` for thread synchronization, as it lacks atomicity and cross-thread memory barriers.

failureModes.name: Pointer-Chasing & `consume` Illusion
failureModes.description: Assuming reading a pointer automatically orders reading the struct it points to. On DEC Alpha (and under aggressive compiler value-speculation), data-dependent loads can still observe stale struct fields.
failureModes.mitigation: Use `memory_order_acquire` on the pointer load (compilers treat `memory_order_consume` as `acquire` anyway due to dependency-tracking fragility).

failureModes.name: Torn 64-Bit Reads on 32-Bit / Unaligned Targets
failureModes.description: Writing a 64-bit `long` or `double` without synchronization on 32-bit architectures or across 64-byte cache-line boundaries splits the write into two 32-bit stores, allowing readers to see half-old, half-new bits.
failureModes.mitigation: Align all atomic variables to their natural size (`alignas(8)` for 64-bit) and access them exclusively through language atomic primitives.

commonMistakes: Assuming MESI cache coherence alone guarantees cross-variable ordering (MESI only orders writes to a single cache line, not across store buffers and invalidation queues).
Using C/C++ `volatile` for inter-thread communication instead of `std::atomic` (`volatile` is for MMIO hardware registers and prevents compiler caching, not CPU reordering).
Testing lock-free code only on x86-64 and assuming it is portable to ARM64 servers or mobile devices.
Mixing `relaxed` and `seq_cst` operations on the same atomic variable without verifying whether `seq_cst`'s total order still holds.
Forgetting that `std::atomic<T>` only synchronizes when the *same* atomic variable is written with `release` and read with `acquire` (no transitive synchronization via unrelated variables).

sections.content:
## The idea

Hardware and compilers do not execute your code in the exact sequence you wrote it. Compilers reorder independent instructions to maximize register reuse and instruction-level parallelism, while CPU cores buffer writes in **store buffers** (56–72 entries deep) and defer cache invalidations in **invalidation queues** so the ALU doesn't stall for 40–100 ns waiting on other cores.

A **memory model** is the formal contract between programmer, compiler, and hardware specifying which reorderings are legal. Its core building block is **happens-before (`->hb`)**: a strict partial order created by combining single-thread *sequenced-before* order with cross-thread *synchronizes-with* edges (such as a `release` store observed by an `acquire` load, or a mutex `unlock` followed by `lock`). If write `W` happens-before read `R`, the system guarantees `R` sees `W` (or a later write)—even if `W` and `R` touched completely different memory addresses.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a classic message-passing handoff between Writer (Core 0) and Reader (Core 1) on an ARMv8 CPU:

1. **Payload write:** Core 0 writes `data = 42` to a non-atomic struct. The write sits in Core 0's store buffer; Core 1's L1 cache still holds `data = 0`.
2. **Release publication:** Core 0 executes `ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release)` (ARM `STLR`). The `release` barrier forbids the CPU and compiler from reordering `data = 42` *after* `ready = true`.
3. **Coherence propagation:** Core 0's store buffer drains in FIFO order: first `data = 42` acquires ownership (MESI Modified) via Read-For-Ownership (RFO), then `ready = true` becomes globally visible.
4. **Acquire observation:** Core 1 spins on `while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire))` (ARM `LDAR`). Once Core 1 reads `true`, the `acquire` barrier forbids any subsequent read of `data` from executing *before* `ready` was observed.
5. **Guaranteed visibility:** Because `data = 42` sequenced-before `ready = true` (release) synchronizes-with `ready == true` (acquire) sequenced-before `print(data)`, `data = 42` **happens-before** `print(data)`. Reading `0` is mathematically impossible.

data.title: Establishing Happens-Before Across Store Buffers and Cache Coherence

edges.label: 1. Buffer data=42
edges.title: Non-atomic payload store
edges.description: Core 0 writes data=42 into its private store buffer without stalling the execution pipeline.

edges.label: 2. Release barrier
edges.title: Order-preserving flag store
edges.description: ready.store(true, release) emits STLR/barrier, preventing data=42 from draining after ready=true.

edges.label: 3. Drain & RFO
edges.title: Coherence commit
edges.description: Store buffer drains data=42 then ready=true to L1 cache, invalidating stale lines on other cores.

edges.label: 4. Acquire load
edges.title: Synchronizes-with edge
edges.description: Core 1 executes ready.load(acquire) (LDAR) and observes true, forming the cross-thread happens-before edge.

edges.label: 5. Process inv queue
edges.title: Flush stale reads
edges.description: The acquire barrier ensures Core 1 processes pending cache invalidations before issuing subsequent loads.

edges.label: 6. Read data == 42
edges.title: Consistent payload read
edges.description: Core 1 loads data from coherent cache and is guaranteed to see 42, never 0.

data.caption: Release/acquire barriers force store buffers and invalidation queues to respect program order across independent memory locations.

sections.content:
## Language models vs. hardware models

Every high-level language compiles its memory model down to the weakest target CPU it supports:

- **C++11/20 & Rust:** Share the DRF-SC (Data-Race-Free implies Sequential Consistency) model. Any program free of data races behaves as if sequentially consistent when using `seq_cst`, while `acquire`/`release` and `relaxed` unlock hardware-specific speedups.
- **Java Memory Model (JMM, JSR-133):** Guarantees no out-of-thin-air values even under benign-looking races, gives `volatile` fields `seq_cst`-like release/acquire semantics, and provides a special happens-before guarantee for `final` fields initialized in a constructor.
- **Go Memory Model:** Updated in Go 1.19 to explicitly specify `sync/atomic` operations as sequentially consistent; recommends channel communication (`send` happens-before `receive` completes) over raw shared memory.

## Memory ordering & hardware mapping

| Ordering Mode | Reordering Prevented | x86-64 Instruction | ARMv8 Instruction | Typical Cost (Uncontended) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`relaxed`** | None (atomicity only) | `MOV` | `LDR` / `STR` | ~0.5–1 ns |
| **`acquire`** | Later reads/writes cannot move before load | `MOV` (compiler barrier) | `LDAR` | ~1–4 ns |
| **`release`** | Earlier reads/writes cannot move after store | `MOV` (compiler barrier) | `STLR` | ~1–4 ns |
| **`acq_rel`** | Both `acquire` and `release` on RMW | `LOCK XADD` / `CMPXCHG` | `LDAXR` / `STLXR` | ~6–15 ns |
| **`seq_cst`** | Total global order across all `seq_cst` ops | `XCHG` / `MFENCE` | `LDAR` / `STLR` + barrier | ~15–40 ns |

## Failure modes

**1. The x86-to-ARM migration trap:** Because x86-64's TSO hardware preserves `acquire` and `release` semantics on regular `MOV` instructions, missing barriers often go undetected for years until an ARM64 port triggers sporadic heisenbugs.

**2. ABA & memory reclamation races:** Even with `seq_cst` atomics, freeing a node in a lock-free stack while another thread holds a stale pointer to it causes use-after-free unless paired with hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation.

**3. False sharing masquerading as barrier overhead:** Placing two `std::atomic` counters within the same 64-byte cache line forces constant MESI Read-For-Ownership traffic across cores, degrading throughput by 10–30x regardless of whether you use `relaxed` or `seq_cst`.

## Testing and formal verification

Stress-testing concurrent code on a single CPU architecture rarely exposes weak-memory bugs. Use deterministic model checkers that systematically explore all valid thread interleavings and store-buffer reorderings:

- **Rust:** Run `loom` (`loom::sync::atomic`) in unit tests to exhaustively permute `relaxed`/`acquire`/`release` schedules.
- **C/C++:** Compile with ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread`) for dynamic happens-before race detection, and use `GenMC` or `CDSChecker` for stateless model checking of lock-free algorithms.
- **Java:** Use `jcstress` (Java Concurrency Stress) on both x86 and ARM64 hosts to empirically detect forbidden outcomes.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Default to `Mutex`, `RwLock`, or channels; drop down to lock-free atomics only when profiling proves lock contention.
- [ ] Never use plain non-atomic variables or C/C++ `volatile` for cross-thread signaling—always use `std::atomic`, Java `volatile`/`VarHandle`, or `sync/atomic`.
- [ ] Pair every `release` store with an `acquire` load on the **same** atomic variable to establish a valid synchronizes-with edge.
- [ ] Align contended per-thread atomic counters to 64 bytes (`alignas(64)`) to eliminate MESI cache-line bouncing.
- [ ] Run ThreadSanitizer (`TSan`), `loom`, or `jcstress` on ARM64 CI runners before shipping lock-free code.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Memory Models Happens Before

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A memory model defines the exact rules under which writes by one CPU core become visible to another, using a formal partial order called happens-before to constrain compiler reordering, CPU store buffers, and out-of-order execution.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: L1/L2 Cache (MESI) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Core 1 (Reader).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Core 1 (Reader) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use `memory_order_seq_cst` (which flushes the store buffer via `LOCK`/`MFENCE` on x86) whenever two threads must observe each other's writes in a mutually exclusive pattern.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Cache coherence (MESI) guarantees cores eventually agree on a single address, not the order of writes across different addresses; only explicit happens-before edges (release/acquire, mutexes, volatile) prevent stale reads on ARM and x86.
Avoid trap: Assuming MESI cache coherence alone guarantees cross-variable ordering (MESI only orders writes to a single cache line, not across store buffers and invalidation queues).
Avoid trap: Using C/C++ `volatile` for inter-thread communication instead of `std::atomic` (`volatile` is for MMIO hardware registers and prevents compiler caching, not CPU reordering).
When to reach for it: Implementing lock-free data structures (ring buffers, SPSC/MPSC queues, epoch-based reclamation) using `std::atomic` or Java `VarHandle`.
When to reach for it: Publishing immutable configuration snapshots or lookup tables via atomic pointer swaps (`release` store paired with `acquire` load) without taking a reader lock.

putItTogether.title: Putting Memory Models Happens Before Together
putItTogether.summary: Cache coherence (MESI) guarantees cores eventually agree on a single address, not the order of writes across different addresses; only explicit happens-before edges (release/acquire, mutexes, volatile) prevent stale reads on ARM and x86.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Memory Models Happens Before before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: After migrating to AWS Graviton3 (ARM64), consumers intermittently read zeroed/stale payloads because ARM reordered the `head` index store ahead of the payload write. Changing `head` to `release`/`acquire` fixed the corruption with <1% throughput impact.
